section.title: Alternating series

exercise.title: Why can organized cancellation save a series?

statement.p: The harmonic series diverges, but the alternating harmonic series converges. In your own words, why do the partial sums bounce across a narrowing gap, and why is that a different mechanism from the positive-series tests?

hint.p: Each new term partially undoes the last one, and the corrections get smaller. Positive tests have no cancellation to use; here the cancellation is the engine.

exercise.title: Why do both Alternating Series Test hypotheses matter?

statement.p: The Alternating Series Test needs decreasing term sizes and terms approaching zero. In your own words, why do alternating signs alone fail, and why can terms going to zero still fail if the sizes are not decreasing in an organized way?

hint.p: Without sizes going to zero, the bounce never shrinks. Without decreasing sizes, a later positive lump can be larger than the previous correction, and the paired sums can still diverge.

subsection.title: Conditional convergence
subsection.p: The alternating harmonic series converges:
converges.
But the positive series made from the absolute values is the harmonic series:
and this diverges.
So the convergence of the alternating harmonic series depends on cancellation. If we remove the signs, it falls apart.
Thus
Conditional convergence is useful, but delicate. It depends on a balance between positive and negative terms.
This delicacy is one reason we next study absolute convergence, which is safer. If a series converges even after all signs are made positive, then it does not need cancellation to survive.

statement.p: A series converges conditionally if it converges, but the series of absolute values diverges. In your own words, why does that mean the convergence depends on cancellation, and why is a safer kind of convergence waiting in the next section?

hint.p: Remove the signs and the harmonic series reappears. Survival that requires a balance of plus and minus is useful, but it is not the same as having finite total size.
